<reason>Both sides ran a disciplined, well-structured debate with proper Q/A formatting and no evidence-rule violations, but CON built the more layered and ultimately more persuasive case. CON's defaults/inertia mechanism was well-grounded in ordinary background knowledge and never squarely rebutted—PRO conceded defaults matter but never showed why casual users would actually flip the switch. CON then converted PRO's repeated concession that engagement-driven ranking "survives intact" for opted-in users into a decisive weighing frame: PRO's policy redistributes exposure to the already-mobilized without fixing the underlying harm, while CON's alternative (fix ranking, keep incidental exposure) claims to capture the same benefit without the new inequality. PRO's best counter—that ranking fixes are orthogonal to the default question—was clever but never fully exploited to independently justify opt-in on its own terms; PRO mostly retreated to "reduced exposure is itself a benefit" without closing the loop on the civic-cost side. CON's classification/marginalized-voices point and concentration-of-partisans argument added texture PRO addressed but didn't neutralize (PRO's "not deleted, just less reach" concession still grants a real cost). PRO's sharpest pressure question (composition shift ≠ societal polarization) exposed a real gap, and CON's answer partially dodged into vaguer "civic silence" language, but PRO's closing didn't fully capitalize on that opening. Overall CON's synthesis was more vivid, better integrated across rounds, and left PRO's central redemption move (that reduced unsolicited amplification is inherently sufficient benefit) resting on an unweighed assumption.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over [B4.1]-[A4.1]/[A4.2], where CON forced PRO to admit the opt-in rule leaves engagement-driven ranking fully intact for opted-in users, and PRO's ranking-orthogonality response in [B4.2]/[B4.5], was the decisive clash—PRO's "reduced exposure is itself the benefit" answer never fully offset CON's redistribution-of-harm framing.</best_rebuttal>
